questions.q: During a market crash, FIIs suddenly sell large amounts of Indian stocks. Why does this often cause the Nifty to fall harder than it would from retail selling alone?
options: FIIs own a large portion of market cap, so their selling creates immediate supply that outpaces demand
FIIs have access to insider information that retail investors don't have
The RBI automatically reduces interest rates when FIIs sell
Retail investors are required by law to follow FII trading decisions
questions.explain: FIIs control significant market share; their large-volume exits create a liquidity imbalance that pushes prices down faster than smaller retail trades would.

questions.q: You buy 100 shares of TCS at ₹3,000 per share. The next day, Nifty rises 2% but TCS only rises 1%. What does this most likely tell you?
options: TCS will fall tomorrow because it underperformed today
TCS is less volatile (or more defensive) than the overall market; it moves less with broad market swings
You should sell TCS immediately to avoid losses
The market is overvalued and TCS is correctly priced
questions.explain: A stock moving less than the index suggests lower volatility or beta—it responds less to market movements, which is typical of stable, large-cap stocks.

questions.q: You start a ₹5,000 monthly SIP in a mutual fund when the NAV is ₹100. Next month the NAV falls to ₹90. Why might this actually benefit you in the long run?
options: The fund manager will lower fees because the NAV dropped
Your second ₹5,000 buys more units at the lower price, lowering your average cost and maximizing rupee-cost averaging
A falling NAV guarantees the fund will recover to ₹100 within one year
The RBI will intervene to support mutual fund prices
questions.explain: SIPs buy more units when prices are low and fewer when high, automatically lowering your average acquisition cost over time—a key benefit of systematic investing.

questions.q: You own a bond with a 6% coupon. The RBI raises interest rates, and new bonds now offer 8% coupons. What happens to the market price of your bond?
options: It stays the same because the coupon is fixed
It rises because higher rates make all bonds more attractive
It falls because investors can now get better returns elsewhere, reducing demand for your lower-yielding bond
It doubles because the interest rate increase applies retroactively to existing bonds
questions.explain: When new bonds offer higher yields, older bonds with lower coupons become less attractive and must trade at a discount to compete—inverse relationship between rates and bond prices.

questions.q: You buy a stock for ₹1,000 and sell it for ₹1,500 after 18 months. How is your gain taxed in India?
options: As long-term capital gain at 20% with indexation benefit, reducing your taxable gain
As income under slab rates (up to 30%), the same as salary
As short-term capital gain at 15%, with no indexation
No tax, because gains under ₹2 lakhs are always exempt
questions.explain: Equity held over 12 months qualifies for long-term capital gains tax at 20% with indexation benefit, which adjusts the cost for inflation—more favorable than short-term or income tax.
